muscle-protein-synthesis.short: Building new muscle protein from amino acids. Measured as the % of muscle protein made new per hour (about 0.03–0.1 %·h⁻¹). Exercise and eating protein both raise it.

muscle-protein-breakdown.short: Taking muscle proteins apart into amino acids, so old or damaged ones are cleared. It runs all the time, alongside building.

myofibrillar-protein.short: The proteins of the myofibrils, the threads that contract (mainly actin and myosin). More of it means bigger, stronger fibres.

mitochondrial-protein.short: The proteins that make up the mitochondria, including their enzymes for burning fuel with oxygen. Endurance training adds more of them.

essential-amino-acid.short: One of the 9 amino acids the body cannot make, so they must come from food. Building muscle protein needs all of them.

leucine.short: An essential amino acid that also works as a signal: a rise in blood leucine after a meal helps switch on muscle protein building (through mTOR).

whey.short: The protein in the watery part of milk (about 20% of milk protein). Digested fast and rich in leucine (about 11%).

casein.short: The main protein of milk (about 80%) and of cheese and quark. It clumps in the stomach, so it is digested slowly and releases amino acids over hours.

glycogen-synthase.short: The enzyme that adds glucose to glycogen chains: the step that sets how fast glycogen is rebuilt. Low glycogen, recent contraction and insulin all speed it up.

fructose.short: 'Fruit sugar': a simple sugar like glucose but absorbed from the gut by a different carrier and handled mostly by the liver. Half of table sugar is fructose.

sucrose.short: Table sugar: one glucose joined to one fructose. The gut splits it quickly, so it acts like a glucose–fructose mix.

rda.short: The daily intake of a nutrient that covers the needs of almost all healthy people. For protein it is 0.8 g per kg body mass per day, set for the general population.

iaao.short: A tracer method for protein needs: a labelled amino acid is given and its burning (labelled CO₂ in breath) falls as protein intake rises, then levels off. That bend point is read as the need (debated).
